verses.textLatin: ne forte insultet tibi cum audierit, et exprobrare non cesset. Gratia et amicitia liberant: quas tibi serva, ne exprobrabilis fias.

verses.text: To speak a word in due time, is like apples of gold on beds of silver.
verses.textLatin: Mala aurea in lectis argenteis, qui loquitur verbum in tempore suo.

verses.text: As an earring of gold and a bright pearl, so is he that reproveth the wise, and the obedient ear.
verses.textLatin: Inauris aurea, et margaritum fulgens, qui arguit sapientem et aurem obedientem.

verses.text: As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to him that sent him, for he refresheth his soul.
verses.textLatin: Sicut frigus nivis in die messis, ita legatus fidelis ei qui misit eum: animam ipsius requiescere facit.

verses.text: As clouds, and wind, when no rain followeth, so is the man that boasteth, and doth not fulfil his promises.
verses.textLatin: Nubes, et ventus, et pluviæ non sequentes, vir gloriosus et promissa non complens.

verses.text: By patience a prince shall be appeased, and a soft tongue shall break hardness.
verses.textLatin: Patientia lenietur princeps, et lingua mollis confringet duritiam.

verses.text: Thou hast found honey, eat what is sufficient for thee, lest being glutted therewith thou vomit it up.
verses.textLatin: Mel invenisti: comede quod sufficit tibi, ne forte satiatus evomas illud.

verses.text: Withdraw thy foot from the house of thy neighbour, lest having his fill he hate thee.
verses.textLatin: Subtrahe pedem tuum de domo proximi tui, nequando satiatus oderit te.

verses.text: A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour, is like a dart and a sword and a sharp arrow.
verses.textLatin: Jaculum, et gladius, et sagitta acuta, homo qui loquitur contra proximum suum falsum testimonium.

verses.text: To trust to an unfaithful man in the time of trouble, is like a rotten tooth, and weary foot,
verses.textLatin: Dens putridus, et pes lassus, qui sperat super infideli in die angustiæ,

verses.text: And one that looseth his garment in cold weather. As vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to a very evil heart. As a moth doth by a garment, and a worm by the wood: so the sadness of a man consumeth the heart.
verses.textLatin: et amittit pallium in die frigoris. Acetum in nitro, qui cantat carmina cordi pessimo. Sicut tinea vestimento, et vermis ligno, ita tristitia viri nocet cordi.

verses.text: If thy enemy be hungry, give him to eat: if he thirst, give him water to drink:
verses.textLatin: Si esurierit inimicus tuus, ciba illum; si sitierit, da ei aquam bibere:

verses.text: For thou shalt heap hot coals upon his head, and the Lord will reward thee.
verses.textLatin: prunas enim congregabis super caput ejus, et Dominus reddet tibi.

verses.text: The north wind driveth away rain, as doth a sad countenance a backbiting tongue.
verses.textLatin: Ventus aquilo dissipat pluvias, et facies tristis linguam detrahentem.

verses.text: It is better to sit in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman, and in a common house.
verses.textLatin: Melius est sedere in angulo domatis quam cum muliere litigiosa et in domo communi.

verses.text: As cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good tidings from a far country.
verses.textLatin: Aqua frigida animæ sitienti, et nuntius bonus de terra longinqua.

verses.text: A just man falling down before the wicked, is as a fountain troubled with the foot, and a corrupted spring.
verses.textLatin: Fons turbatus pede et vena corrupta, justus cadens coram impio.

verses.text: As it is not good for a man to eat much honey, so he that is a searcher of majesty, shall be overwhelmed by glory.
verses.textLatin: Sicut qui mel multum comedit non est ei bonum, sic qui scrutator est majestatis opprimetur a gloria.

verses.text: As a city that lieth open and is not compassed with walls, so is a man that cannot refrain his own spirit in speaking.
verses.textLatin: Sicut urbs patens et absque murorum ambitu, ita vir qui non potest in loquendo cohibere spiritum suum.

verses.text: As  snow in summer, and rain in harvest, so glory is not seemly for a fool.
verses.textLatin: Quomodo nix in æstate, et pluviæ in messe, sic indecens est stulto gloria.

verses.text: As a bird flying to other places, and a sparrow going here or there: so a curse uttered without cause shall come upon a man.
verses.textLatin: Sicut avis ad alia transvolans, et passer quolibet vadens, sic maledictum frustra prolatum in quempiam superveniet.

verses.text: A whip for a horse, and a snaffle for an ass, and a rod for the back of fools.
verses.textLatin: Flagellum equo, et camus asino, et virga in dorso imprudentium.

verses.text: Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou be made like him.
verses.textLatin: Ne respondeas stulto juxta stultitiam suam, ne efficiaris ei similis.

verses.text: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he imagine himself to be wise.
verses.textLatin: Responde stulto juxta stultitiam suam, ne sibi sapiens esse videatur.

verses.text: He that sendeth words by a foolish messenger, is lame of feet and drinketh iniquity.
verses.textLatin: Claudus pedibus, et iniquitatem bibens, qui mittit verba per nuntium stultum.

verses.text: As a lame man hath fair legs in vain: so a parable is unseemly in the mouth of fools.
verses.textLatin: Quomodo pulchras frustra habet claudus tibias, sic indecens est in ore stultorum parabola.

verses.text: As he that casteth a stone into the heap of Mercury: so is he that giveth honour to a fool.
verses.textLatin: Sicut qui mittit lapidem in acervum Mercurii, ita qui tribuit insipienti honorem.

verses.text: As if a thorn should grow in the hand of a drunkard: so is a parable in the mouth of fools.
verses.textLatin: Quomodo si spina nascatur in manu temulenti, sic parabola in ore stultorum.

verses.text: Judgment determineth causes: and he that putteth a fool to silence, appeaseth anger.
verses.textLatin: Judicium determinat causas, et qui imponit stulto silentium iras mitigat.

verses.text: As a dog that returneth to his vomit, so is the fool that repeateth his folly.
verses.textLatin: Sicut canis qui revertitur ad vomitum suum, sic imprudens qui iterat stultitiam suam.

verses.text: Hast thou seen a man wise in his own conceit? there shall be more hope of a fool than of him.
verses.textLatin: Vidisti hominem sapientem sibi videri? magis illo spem habebit insipiens.

verses.text: The slothful man saith: There is a lion in the way, and a lioness in the roads.
verses.textLatin: Dicit piger: Leo est in via, et leæna in itineribus.

verses.text: As the door turneth upon its hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed.
verses.textLatin: Sicut ostium vertitur in cardine suo, ita piger in lectulo suo.

verses.text: The slothful hideth his hand under his armpit, and it grieveth him to turn it to his mouth.
verses.textLatin: Abscondit piger manum sub ascella sua, et laborat si ad os suum eam converterit.

verses.text: The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit, than seven men that speak sentences.
verses.textLatin: Sapientior sibi piger videtur septem viris loquentibus sententias.

verses.text: As he that taketh a dog by the ears, so is he that passeth by in anger, and meddleth with another man’s quarrel.
verses.textLatin: Sicut qui apprehendit auribus canem, sic qui transit impatiens et commiscetur rixæ alterius.

verses.text: As he is guilty that shooteth arrows, and lances unto death:
verses.textLatin: Sicut noxius est qui mittit sagittas et lanceas in mortem,

verses.text: So is the man that hurteth his friend deceitfully: and when he is taken, saith: I did it in jest.
verses.textLatin: ita vir fraudulenter nocet amico suo, et cum fuerit deprehensus dicit: Ludens feci.

verses.text: When the wood faileth, the fire shall go out: and when the talebearer is taken away, contentions shall cease.
verses.textLatin: Cum defecerint ligna extinguetur ignis, et susurrone subtracto, jurgia conquiescent.

verses.text: As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire, so an angry man stirreth up strife.
verses.textLatin: Sicut carbones ad prunas, et ligna ad ignem, sic homo iracundus suscitat rixas.

verses.text: The words of a talebearer are as it were simple, but they reach to the innermost parts of the belly.
verses.textLatin: Verba susurronis quasi simplicia, et ipsa perveniunt ad intima ventris.

verses.text: Swelling lips joined with a corrupt heart, are like an earthen vessel adorned with silver dross.
verses.textLatin: Quomodo si argento sordido ornare velis vas fictile, sic labia tumentia cum pessimo corde sociata.

verses.text: An enemy is known by his lips, when in his heart he entertaineth deceit.
verses.textLatin: Labiis suis intelligitur inimicus, cum in corde tractaverit dolos.

verses.text: When he shall speak low, trust him not: because there are seven mischiefs in his heart.
verses.textLatin: Quando submiserit vocem suam, ne credideris ei, quoniam septem nequitiæ sunt in corde illius.

verses.text: He that covereth hatred deceitfully, his malice shall be laid open in the public assembly.
verses.textLatin: Qui operit odium fraudulenter, revelabitur malitia ejus in consilio.

verses.text: He that diggeth a pit, shall fall into it: and he that rolleth a stone, it shall return to him.
verses.textLatin: Qui fodit foveam incidet in eam, et qui volvit lapidem revertetur ad eum.

verses.text: A deceitful tongue loveth not truth: and a slippery mouth worketh ruin.
verses.textLatin: Lingua fallax non amat veritatem, et os lubricum operatur ruinas.

verses.text: Boast  not for to morrow, for thou knowest not what the day to come may bring forth.
verses.textLatin: Ne glorieris in crastinum, ignorans quid superventura pariat dies.

verses.text: Let another praise thee, and not thy own mouth: a stranger, and not thy own lips.
verses.textLatin: Laudet te alienus, et non os tuum; extraneus, et non labia tua.

verses.text: A stone is heavy, and sand weighty: but the anger of a fool is heavier than them both.
verses.textLatin: Grave est saxum, et onerosa arena, sed ira stulti utroque gravior.

verses.text: Anger hath no mercy, nor fury when it breaketh forth: and who can bear the violence of one provoked?
verses.textLatin: Ira non habet misericordiam nec erumpens furor, et impetum concitati ferre quis poterit?

verses.text: Open rebuke is better than hidden love.
verses.textLatin: Melior est manifesta correptio quam amor absconditus.

verses.text: Better are the wounds of a friend, than the deceitful kisses of an enemy.
verses.textLatin: Meliora sunt vulnera diligentis quam fraudulenta oscula odientis.

verses.text: A soul that is full shall tread upon the honeycomb: and a soul that is hungry shall take even bitter for sweet.
verses.textLatin: Anima saturata calcabit favum, et anima esuriens etiam amarum pro dulci sumet.

verses.text: As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that leaveth his place.
verses.textLatin: Sicut avis transmigrans de nido suo, sic vir qui derelinquit locum suum.

verses.text: Ointment and perfumes rejoice the heart: and the good counsels of a friend are sweet to the soul.
verses.textLatin: Unguento et variis odoribus delectatur cor, et bonis amici consiliis anima dulcoratur.

verses.text: Thy own friend, and thy father’s friend forsake not: and go not into thy brother’s house in the day of thy affliction. Better is a neighbour that is near, than a brother afar off.
verses.textLatin: Amicum tuum et amicum patris tui ne dimiseris, et domum fratris tui ne ingrediaris in die afflictionis tuæ. Melior est vicinus juxta quam frater procul.

verses.text: Study wisdom, my son, and make my heart joyful, that thou mayst give an answer to him that reproacheth.
verses.textLatin: Stude sapientiæ, fili mi, et lætifica cor meum, ut possis exprobranti respondere sermonem.

verses.text: The prudent man seeing evil hideth himself: little ones passing on have suffered losses.
verses.textLatin: Astutus videns malum, absconditus est: parvuli transeuntes sustinuerunt dispendia.

verses.text: Take away his garment that hath been surety for a stranger: and take from him a pledge for strangers.
verses.textLatin: Tolle vestimentum ejus qui spopondit pro extraneo, et pro alienis aufer ei pignus.

verses.text: He that blesseth his neighbour with a loud voice, rising in the night, shall be like to him that curseth.
verses.textLatin: Qui benedicit proximo suo voce grandi, de nocte consurgens maledicenti similis erit.

verses.text: Roofs dropping through in a cold day, and a contentious woman are alike.
verses.textLatin: Tecta perstillantia in die frigoris et litigiosa mulier comparantur.

verses.text: He that retaineth her, is as he that would hold the wind, and shall call in the oil of his right hand.
verses.textLatin: Qui retinet eam quasi qui ventum teneat, et oleum dexteræ suæ vocabit.

verses.text: Iron sharpeneth iron, so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
verses.textLatin: Ferrum ferro exacuitur, et homo exacuit faciem amici sui.

verses.text: He that keepeth the fig tree, shall eat the fruit thereof: and he that is the keeper of his master, shall be glorified.
verses.textLatin: Qui servat ficum comedet fructus ejus, et qui custos est domini sui glorificabitur.

verses.text: As the faces of them that look therein, shine in the water, so the hearts of men are laid open to the wise.
verses.textLatin: Quomodo in aquis resplendent vultus prospicientium, sic corda hominum manifesta sunt prudentibus.

verses.text: Hell and destruction are never filled: so the eyes of men are never satisfied.
verses.textLatin: Infernus et perditio numquam implentur: similiter et oculi hominum insatiabiles.

verses.text: As silver is tried in the fining-pot and gold in the furnace: so a man is tried by the mouth of him that praiseth. The heart of the wicked seeketh after evils, but the righteous heart seeketh after knowledge.
verses.textLatin: Quomodo probatur in conflatorio argentum et in fornace aurum, sic probatur homo ore laudantis. Cor iniqui inquirit mala, cor autem rectum inquirit scientiam.

verses.text: Though thou shouldst bray a fool in the mortar, as when a pestle striketh upon sodden barley, his folly would not be taken from him.
verses.textLatin: Si contuderis stultum in pila quasi ptisanas feriente desuper pilo, non auferetur ab eo stultitia ejus.

verses.text: Be diligent to know the countenance of thy cattle, and consider thy own flocks:
verses.textLatin: Diligenter agnosce vultum pecoris tui, tuosque greges considera:

verses.text: For thou shalt not always have power: but a crown shall be given to generation and generation.
verses.textLatin: non enim habebis jugiter potestatem, sed corona tribuetur in generationem et generationem.

verses.text: The meadows are open, and the green herbs have appeared, and the hay is gathered out of the mountains.
verses.textLatin: Aperta sunt prata, et apparuerunt herbæ virentes, et collecta sunt fœna de montibus.

verses.text: Lambs are for thy clothing: and kids for the price of the field.
verses.textLatin: Agni ad vestimentum tuum, et hædi ad agri pretium.

verses.text: Let the milk of the goats be enough for thy food, and for the necessities of thy house, and for maintenance for thy handmaids.
verses.textLatin: Sufficiat tibi lac caprarum in cibos tuos, et in necessaria domus tuæ, et ad victum ancillis tuis.

verses.text: The  wicked man fleeth, when no man pursueth: but the just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread.
verses.textLatin: Fugit impius nemine persequente; justus autem, quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit.

verses.text: For the sins of the land many are the princes thereof: and for the wisdom of a man, and the knowledge of those things that are said, the life of the prince shall be prolonged.
verses.textLatin: Propter peccata terræ multi principes ejus; et propter hominis sapientiam, et horum scientiam quæ dicuntur, vita ducis longior erit.

verses.text: A poor man that oppresseth the poor, is like a violent shower, which bringeth a famine.
verses.textLatin: Vir pauper calumnians pauperes similis est imbri vehementi in quo paratur fames.

verses.text: They that forsake the law, praise the wicked man: they that keep it, are incensed against him.
verses.textLatin: Qui derelinquunt legem laudant impium; qui custodiunt, succenduntur contra eum.

verses.text: Evil men think not on judgment: but they that seek after the Lord, take notice of all things.
verses.textLatin: Viri mali non cogitant judicium; qui autem inquirunt Dominum animadvertunt omnia.

verses.text: Better is the poor man walking in his simplicity, than the rich in crooked ways.
verses.textLatin: Melior est pauper ambulans in simplicitate sua quam dives in pravis itineribus.

verses.text: He that keepeth the law is a wise son: but he that feedeth gluttons, shameth his father.
verses.textLatin: Qui custodit legem filius sapiens est; qui autem comessatores pascit confundit patrem suum.

verses.text: He that heapeth together riches by usury and loan, gathereth them for him that will be bountiful to the poor.
verses.textLatin: Qui coacervat divitias usuris et fœnore, liberali in pauperes congregat eas.

verses.text: He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination.
verses.textLatin: Qui declinat aures suas ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit execrabilis.

verses.text: He that deceiveth the just in a wicked way, shall fall in his own destruction: and the upright shall possess his goods.
verses.textLatin: Qui decipit justos in via mala, in interitu suo corruet, et simplices possidebunt bona ejus.

verses.text: The rich man seemeth to himself wise: but the poor man that is prudent shall search him out.
verses.textLatin: Sapiens sibi videtur vir dives; pauper autem prudens scrutabitur eum.

verses.text: In the joy of the just there is great glory: when the wicked reign, men are ruined.
verses.textLatin: In exsultatione justorum multa gloria est; regnantibus impiis, ruinæ hominum.

verses.text: He that hideth his sins, shall not prosper: but he that shall confess, and forsake them, shall obtain mercy.
verses.textLatin: Qui abscondit scelera sua non dirigetur; qui autem confessus fuerit et reliquerit ea, misericordiam consequetur.

verses.text: Blessed is the man that is always fearful: but he that is hardened in mind, shall fall into evil.
verses.textLatin: Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus; qui vero mentis est duræ corruet in malum.

verses.text: As a roaring lion, and a hungry bear, so is a wicked prince over the poor people.
verses.textLatin: Leo rugiens et ursus esuriens, princeps impius super populum pauperem.

verses.text: A prince void of prudence shall oppress many by calumny: but he that hateth covetousness, shall prolong his days.
verses.textLatin: Dux indigens prudentia multos opprimet per calumniam; qui autem odit avaritiam, longi fient dies ejus.

verses.text: A man that doth violence to the blood of a person, if he flee even to the pit, no man will stay him.
verses.textLatin: Hominem qui calumniatur animæ sanguinem, si usque ad lacum fugerit, nemo sustinet.

verses.text: He that walketh uprightly, shall be saved: he that is perverse in his ways shall fall at once.
verses.textLatin: Qui ambulat simpliciter salvus erit; qui perversis graditur viis concidet semel.

verses.text: He that tilleth his ground, shall be filled with bread: but he that followeth idleness shall be filled with poverty.
verses.textLatin: Qui operatur terram suam satiabitur panibus; qui autem sectatur otium replebitur egestate.

verses.text: A faithful man shall be much praised: but he that maketh haste to be rich, shall not be innocent.
verses.textLatin: Vir fidelis multum laudabitur; qui autem festinat ditari non erit innocens.

verses.text: He that hath respect to a person in judgment, doth not well: such a man even for a morsel of bread forsaketh the truth.
verses.textLatin: Qui cognoscit in judicio faciem non bene facit; iste et pro buccella panis deserit veritatem.

verses.text: A man, that maketh haste to be rich, and envieth others, is ignorant that poverty shall come upon him.
verses.textLatin: Vir qui festinat ditari, et aliis invidet, ignorat quod egestas superveniet ei.

verses.text: He that rebuketh a man, shall afterward find favour with him, more than he that by a flattering tongue deceiveth him.
verses.textLatin: Qui corripit hominem gratiam postea inveniet apud eum, magis quam ille qui per linguæ blandimenta decipit.

verses.text: He that stealeth any thing from his father, or from his mother: and saith, This is no sin, is the partner of a murderer.
verses.textLatin: Qui subtrahit aliquid a patre suo et a matre, et dicit hoc non esse peccatum, particeps homicidæ est.
Qui se jactat et dilatat, jurgia concitat; qui vero sperat in Domino sanabitur.

verses.text: He that boasteth, and puffeth up himself, stirreth up quarrels: but he that trusteth in the Lord, shall be healed. He that trusteth in his own heart, is a fool: but he that walketh wisely, he shall be saved.
verses.textLatin: Qui confidit in corde suo stultus est; qui autem graditur sapienter, ipse salvabitur.

verses.text: He that giveth to the poor, shall not want: he that despiseth his entreaty, shall suffer indigence.
verses.textLatin: Qui dat pauperi non indigebit; qui despicit deprecantem sustinebit penuriam.

verses.text: When the wicked rise up, men shall hide themselves: when they perish, the just shall be multiplied.
verses.textLatin: Cum surrexerint impii, abscondentur homines; cum illi perierint, multiplicabuntur justi.

verses.text: The  man that with a stiff neck despiseth him that reproveth him, shall suddenly be destroyed: and health shall not follow him.
verses.textLatin: Viro qui corripientem dura cervice contemnit, repentinus ei superveniet interitus, et eum sanitas non sequetur.

verses.text: When just men increase, the people shall rejoice: when the wicked shall bear rule, the people shall mourn.
verses.textLatin: In multiplicatione justorum lætabitur vulgus; cum impii sumpserint principatum, gemet populus.

verses.text: A man that loveth wisdom, rejoiceth his father: but he that maintaineth harlots, shall squander away his substance.
verses.textLatin: Vir qui amat sapientiam lætificat patrem suum; qui autem nutrit scorta perdet substantiam.

verses.text: A just king setteth up the land: a covetous man shall destroy it.
verses.textLatin: Rex justus erigit terram; vir avarus destruet eam.

verses.text: A man that speaketh to his friend with flattering and dissembling words, spreadeth a net for his feet.
verses.textLatin: Homo qui blandis fictisque sermonibus loquitur amico suo rete expandit gressibus ejus.

verses.text: A snare shall entangle the wicked man when he sinneth: and the just shall praise and rejoice.
verses.textLatin: Peccantem virum iniquum involvet laqueus, et justus laudabit atque gaudebit.

verses.text: The just taketh notice of the cause of the poor: the wicked is void of knowledge.
verses.textLatin: Novit justus causam pauperum; impius ignorat scientiam.

verses.text: Corrupt men bring a city to ruin: but wise men turn away wrath.
verses.textLatin: Homines pestilentes dissipant civitatem; sapientes vero avertunt furorem.

verses.text: If a wise man contend with a fool, whether he be angry, or laugh, he shall find no rest.
verses.textLatin: Vir sapiens si cum stulto contenderit, sive irascatur, sive rideat, non inveniet requiem.

verses.text: Bloodthirsty men hate the upright: but just men seek his soul.
verses.textLatin: Viri sanguinum oderunt simplicem; justi autem quærunt animam ejus.

verses.text: A fool uttereth all his mind: a wise man deferreth, and keepeth it till afterwards.
verses.textLatin: Totum spiritum suum profert stultus; sapiens differt, et reservat in posterum.

verses.text: A prince that gladly heareth lying words, hath all his servants wicked.
verses.textLatin: Princeps qui libenter audit verba mendacii, omnes ministros habet impios.

verses.text: The poor man and the creditor have met one another: the Lord is the enlightener of them both.
verses.textLatin: Pauper et creditor obviaverunt sibi: utriusque illuminator est Dominus.

verses.text: The king that judgeth the poor in truth, his throne shall be established for ever.
verses.textLatin: Rex qui judicat in veritate pauperes, thronus ejus in æternum firmabitur.

verses.text: The rod and reproof give wisdom: but the child that is left to his own will bringeth his mother to shame.
verses.textLatin: Virga atque correptio tribuit sapientiam; puer autem qui dimittitur voluntati suæ confundit matrem suam.

verses.text: When the wicked are multiplied, crimes shall be multiplied: but the just shall see their downfall.
verses.textLatin: In multiplicatione impiorum multiplicabuntur scelera, et justi ruinas eorum videbunt.

verses.text: Instruct thy son, and he shall refresh thee, and shall give delight to thy soul.
verses.textLatin: Erudi filium tuum, et refrigerabit te, et dabit delicias animæ tuæ.

verses.text: When prophecy shall fail, the people shall be scattered abroad: but he that keepeth the law is blessed.
verses.textLatin: Cum prophetia defecerit, dissipabitur populus; qui vero custodit legem beatus est.

verses.text: A slave will not be corrected by words: because he understandeth what thou sayest, and will not answer.
verses.textLatin: Servus verbis non potest erudiri, quia quod dicis intelligit, et respondere contemnit.

verses.text: Hast thou seen a man hasty to speak? folly is rather to be looked for, than his amendment.
verses.textLatin: Vidisti hominem velocem ad loquendum? stultitia magis speranda est quam illius correptio.

verses.text: He that nourisheth his servant delicately from his childhood, afterwards shall find him stubborn.
verses.textLatin: Qui delicate a pueritia nutrit servum suum postea sentiet eum contumacem.

verses.text: A passionate man provoketh quarrels: and he that is easily stirred up to wrath, shall be more prone to sin.
verses.textLatin: Vir iracundus provocat rixas, et qui ad indignandum facilis est erit ad peccandum proclivior.

verses.text: Humiliation followeth the proud: and glory shall uphold the humble of spirit.
verses.textLatin: Superbum sequitur humilitas, et humilem spiritu suscipiet gloria.

verses.text: He that is partaker with a thief, hateth his own soul: he heareth one putting him to his oath, and discovereth not.
verses.textLatin: Qui cum fure participat odit animam suam; adjurantem audit, et non indicat.

verses.text: He that feareth man, shall quickly fall: he that trusteth in the Lord, shall be set on high.
verses.textLatin: Qui timet hominem cito corruet; qui sperat in Domino sublevabitur.

verses.text: Many seek the face of the prince: but the judgment of every one cometh forth from the Lord.
verses.textLatin: Multi requirunt faciem principis, et judicium a Domino egreditur singulorum.

verses.text: The just abhor the wicked man: and the wicked loathe them that are in the right way. The son that keepeth the word, shall be free from destruction.
verses.textLatin: Abominantur justi virum impium, et abominantur impii eos qui in recta sunt via. Verbum custodiens filius extra perditionem erit.

verses.text: The  words of Gatherer the son of Vomiter. The vision which the man spoke with whom God is, and who being strengthened by God, abiding with him, said:
verses.textLatin: Verba Congregantis, filii Vomentis. Visio quam locutus est vir cum quo est Deus, et qui Deo secum morante confortatus, ait:

verses.text: I am the most foolish of men, and the wisdom of men is not with me.
verses.textLatin: Stultissimus sum virorum, et sapientia hominum non est mecum.

verses.text: I have not learned wisdom, and have not known the science of saints.
verses.textLatin: Non didici sapientiam, et non novi scientiam sanctorum.

verses.text: Who hath ascended up into heaven, and descended? who hath held the wind in his hands? who hath bound up the waters together as in a garment? who hath raised up all the borders of the earth? what is his name, and what is the name of his son, if thou knowest?
verses.textLatin: Quis ascendit in cælum, atque descendit? quis continuit spiritum in manibus suis? quis colligavit aquas quasi in vestimento? quis suscitavit omnes terminos terræ? quod nomen est ejus, et quod nomen filii ejus, si nosti?

verses.text: Every word of God is fire tried: he is a buckler to them that hope in him.
verses.textLatin: Omnis sermo Dei ignitus: clypeus est sperantibus in se.

verses.text: Add not any thing to his words, lest thou be reproved, and found a liar:
verses.textLatin: Ne addas quidquam verbis illius, et arguaris, inveniarisque mendax.

verses.text: Two things I have asked of thee, deny them not to me before I die.
verses.textLatin: Duo rogavi te: ne deneges mihi antequam moriar:

verses.text: Remove far from me vanity, and lying words. Give me neither beggary, nor riches: give me only the necessaries of life:
verses.textLatin: vanitatem et verba mendacia longe fac a me; mendicitatem et divitias ne dederis mihi: tribue tantum victui meo necessaria,

verses.text: Lest perhaps being filled, I should be tempted to deny, and say: Who is the Lord? or being compelled by poverty, I should steal, and forswear the name of my God.
verses.textLatin: ne forte satiatus illiciar ad negandum, et dicam: Quis est Dominus? aut egestate compulsus, furer, et perjurem nomen Dei mei.

verses.text: Accuse not a servant to his master, lest he curse thee, and thou fall.
verses.textLatin: Ne accuses servum ad dominum suum, ne forte maledicat tibi, et corruas.

verses.text: There is a generation that curseth their father, and doth not bless their mother.
verses.textLatin: Generatio quæ patri suo maledicit, et quæ matri suæ non benedicit;

verses.text: A generation that are pure in their own eyes, and yet are not washed from their filthiness.
verses.textLatin: generatio quæ sibi munda videtur, et tamen non est lota a sordibus suis;

verses.text: A generation, whose eyes are lofty, and their eyelids lifted up on high.
verses.textLatin: generatio cujus excelsi sunt oculi, et palpebræ ejus in alta surrectæ;

verses.text: A generation, that for teeth hath swords, and grindeth with their jaw teeth, to devour the needy from off the earth, and the poor from among men.
verses.textLatin: generatio quæ pro dentibus gladios habet, et commandit molaribus suis, ut comedat inopes de terra, et pauperes ex hominibus.

verses.text: The horseleech hath two daughters that say: Bring, bring. There are three things that never are satisfied, and the fourth never saith: It is enough.
verses.textLatin: Sanguisugæ duæ sunt filiæ, dicentes: Affer, affer. Tria sunt insaturabilia, et quartum quod numquam dicit: Sufficit.

verses.text: Hell, and the mouth of the womb, and the earth which is not satisfied with water: and the fire never saith: It is enough.
verses.textLatin: Infernus, et os vulvæ, et terra quæ non satiatur aqua: ignis vero numquam dicit: Sufficit.

verses.text: The eye that mocketh at his father, and that despiseth the labour of his mother in bearing him, let the ravens of the brooks pick it out, and the young eagles eat it.
verses.textLatin: Oculum qui subsannat patrem, et qui despicit partum matris suæ, effodiant eum corvi de torrentibus, et comedant eum filii aquilæ!

verses.text: Three things are hard to me, and the fourth I am utterly ignorant of.
verses.textLatin: Tria sunt difficilia mihi, et quartum penitus ignoro:

verses.text: The way of an eagle in the air, the way of a serpent upon a rock, the way of a ship in the midst of the sea, and the way of a man in youth.
verses.textLatin: viam aquilæ in cælo, viam colubri super petram, viam navis in medio mari, et viam viri in adolescentia.

verses.text: Such is also the way of an adulterous woman, who eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith: I have done no evil.
verses.textLatin: Talis est et via mulieris adulteræ, quæ comedit, et tergens os suum dicit: Non sum operata malum.

verses.text: By three things the earth is disturbed, and the fourth it cannot bear:
verses.textLatin: Per tria movetur terra, et quartum non potest sustinere:

verses.text: By a slave when he reigneth: by a fool when he is filled with meat:
verses.textLatin: per servum, cum regnaverit; per stultum, cum saturatus fuerit cibo;

verses.text: By an odious woman when she is married: and by a bondwoman when she is heir to her mistress.
verses.textLatin: per odiosam mulierem, cum in matrimonio fuerit assumpta; et per ancillam, cum fuerit hæres dominæ suæ.

verses.text: There are four very little things of the earth, and they are wiser than the wise:
verses.textLatin: Quatuor sunt minima terræ, et ipsa sunt sapientiora sapientibus:

verses.text: The ants, a feeble people, which provide themselves food in the harvest:
verses.textLatin: formicæ, populus infirmus, qui præparat in messe cibum sibi;

verses.text: The rabbit, a weak people, which maketh its bed in the rock:
verses.textLatin: lepusculus, plebs invalida, qui collocat in petra cubile suum;

verses.text: The locust hath no king, yet they all go out by their bands.
verses.textLatin: regem locusta non habet, et egreditur universa per turmas suas;

verses.text: The stellio supporteth itself on hands, and dwelleth in kings’ houses.
verses.textLatin: stellio manibus nititur, et moratur in ædibus regis.

verses.text: There are three things, which go well, and the fourth that walketh happily:
verses.textLatin: Tria sunt quæ bene gradiuntur, et quartum quod incedit feliciter:

verses.text: A lion, the strongest of beasts, who hath no fear of any thing he meeteth:
verses.textLatin: leo, fortissimus bestiarum, ad nullius pavebit occursum;

verses.text: A cock girded about the loins: and a ram: and a king, whom none can resist.
verses.textLatin: gallus succinctus lumbos; et aries; nec est rex, qui resistat ei.

verses.text: There is that hath appeared a fool after he was lifted up on high: for if he had understood, he would have laid his hand upon his mouth.
verses.textLatin: Est qui stultus apparuit postquam elevatus est in sublime; si enim intellexisset, ori suo imposuisset manum.

verses.text: And he that strongly squeezeth the paps to bring out milk, straineth out butter: and he that violently bloweth his nose, bringeth out blood: and he that provoketh wrath bringeth forth strife.
verses.textLatin: Qui autem fortiter premit ubera ad eliciendum lac exprimit butyrum; et qui vehementer emungit elicit sanguinem; et qui provocat iras producit discordias.

verses.text: The  words of king Lamuel. The vision wherewith his mother instructed him.
verses.textLatin: Verba Lamuelis regis. Visio qua erudivit eum mater sua.

verses.text: What, O my beloved, what, O the beloved of my womb, what, O the beloved of my vows?
verses.textLatin: Quid, dilecte mi? quid, dilecte uteri mei? quid, dilecte votorum meorum?

verses.text: Give not thy substance to women, and thy riches to destroy kings.
verses.textLatin: Ne dederis mulieribus substantiam tuam, et divitias tuas ad delendos reges.

verses.text: Give not to kings, O Lamuel, give not wine to kings: because there is no secret where drunkenness reigneth:
verses.textLatin: Noli regibus, o Lamuel, noli regibus dare vinum, quia nullum secretum est ubi regnat ebrietas;

verses.text: And lest they drink and forget judgments, and pervert the cause of the children of the poor.
verses.textLatin: et ne forte bibant, et obliviscantur judiciorum, et mutent causam filiorum pauperis.

verses.text: Give strong drink to them that are sad: and wine to them that are grieved in mind:
verses.textLatin: Date siceram mœrentibus, et vinum his qui amaro sunt animo.

verses.text: Let them drink, and forget their want, and remember their sorrow no more.
verses.textLatin: Bibant, et obliviscantur egestatis suæ, et doloris sui non recordentur amplius.

verses.text: Open thy mouth for the dumb, and for the causes of all the children that pass.
verses.textLatin: Aperi os tuum muto, et causis omnium filiorum qui pertranseunt.

verses.text: Open thy mouth, decree that which is just, and do justice to the needy and poor.
verses.textLatin: Aperi os tuum, decerne quod justum est, et judica inopem et pauperem.

verses.text: Who shall find a valiant woman? far and from the uttermost coasts is the price of her.
verses.textLatin: Mulierem fortem quis inveniet? procul et de ultimis finibus pretium ejus.

verses.text: The heart of her husband trusteth in her, and he shall have no need of spoils.
verses.textLatin: Confidit in ea cor viri sui, et spoliis non indigebit.

verses.text: She will render him good, and not evil, all the days of her life.
verses.textLatin: Reddet ei bonum, et non malum, omnibus diebus vitæ suæ.

verses.text: She hath sought wool and flax, and hath wrought by the counsel of her hands.
verses.textLatin: Quæsivit lanam et linum, et operata est consilia manuum suarum.

verses.text: She is like the merchant’s ship, she bringeth her bread from afar.
verses.textLatin: Facta est quasi navis institoris, de longe portans panem suum.

verses.text: And she hath risen in the night, and given a prey to her household, and victuals to her maidens.
verses.textLatin: Et de nocte surrexit, deditque prædam domesticis suis, et cibaria ancillis suis.

verses.text: She hath considered a field, and bought it: with the fruit of her hands she hath planted a vineyard.
verses.textLatin: Consideravit agrum, et emit eum; de fructu manuum suarum plantavit vineam.

verses.text: She hath girded her loins with strength, and hath strengthened her arm.
verses.textLatin: Accinxit fortitudine lumbos suos, et roboravit brachium suum.

verses.text: She hath tasted and seen that her traffic is good: her lamp shall not be put out in the night.
verses.textLatin: Gustavit, et vidit quia bona est negotiatio ejus; non extinguetur in nocte lucerna ejus.

verses.text: She hath put out her hand to strong things, and her fingers have taken hold of the spindle.
verses.textLatin: Manum suam misit ad fortia, et digiti ejus apprehenderunt fusum.

verses.text: She hath opened her hand to the needy, and stretched out her hands to the poor.
verses.textLatin: Manum suam aperuit inopi, et palmas suas extendit ad pauperem.

verses.text: She shall not fear for her house in the cold of snow: for all her domestics are clothed with double garments.
verses.textLatin: Non timebit domui suæ a frigoribus nivis; omnes enim domestici ejus vestiti sunt duplicibus.

verses.text: She hath made for herself clothing of tapestry: fine linen, and purple is her covering.
verses.textLatin: Stragulatam vestem fecit sibi; byssus et purpura indumentum ejus.

verses.text: Her husband is honourable in the gates, when he sitteth among the senators of the land.
verses.textLatin: Nobilis in portis vir ejus, quando sederit cum senatoribus terræ.

verses.text: She made fine linen, and sold it, and delivered a girdle to the Chanaanite.
verses.textLatin: Sindonem fecit, et vendidit, et cingulum tradidit Chananæo.

verses.text: Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she shall laugh in the latter day.
verses.textLatin: Fortitudo et decor indumentum ejus, et ridebit in die novissimo.

verses.text: She hath opened her mouth to wisdom, and the law of clemency is on her tongue.
verses.textLatin: Os suum aperuit sapientiæ, et lex clementiæ in lingua ejus.

verses.text: She hath looked well to the paths of her house, and hath not eaten her bread idle.
verses.textLatin: Consideravit semitas domus suæ, et panem otiosa non comedit.

verses.text: Her children rose up, and called her blessed: her husband, and he praised her.
verses.textLatin: Surrexerunt filii ejus, et beatissimam prædicaverunt; vir ejus, et laudavit eam.

verses.text: Many daughters have gathered together riches: thou hast surpassed them all.
verses.textLatin: Multæ filiæ congregaverunt divitias; tu supergressa es universas.

verses.text: Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: the woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.
verses.textLatin: Fallax gratia, et vana est pulchritudo: mulier timens Dominum, ipsa laudabitur.

verses.text: Give her of the fruit of her hands: and let her works praise her in the gates.
verses.textLatin: Date ei de fructu manuum suarum, et laudent eam in portis opera ejus.

verses.text: The  words of Ecclesiastes, the son of David, king of Jerusalem.
verses.textLatin: Verba Ecclesiastæ, filii David, regis Jerusalem.

verses.text: Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes: vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.
verses.textLatin: Vanitas vanitatum, dixit Ecclesiastes; vanitas vanitatum, et omnia vanitas.

verses.text: What hath a man more of all his labour, that he taketh under the sun?
verses.textLatin: Quid habet amplius homo de universo labore suo quo laborat sub sole?

verses.text: One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth standeth for ever.
verses.textLatin: Generatio præterit, et generatio advenit; terra autem in æternum stat.

verses.text: The sun riseth, and goeth down, and returneth to his place: and there rising again,
verses.textLatin: Oritur sol et occidit, et ad locum suum revertitur; ibique renascens,

verses.text: Maketh his round by the south, and turneth again to the north: the spirit goeth forward surveying all places round about, and returneth to his circuits.
verses.textLatin: gyrat per meridiem, et flectitur ad aquilonem. Lustrans universa in circuitu pergit spiritus, et in circulos suos revertitur.

verses.text: All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea doth not overflow: unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return, to flow again.
verses.textLatin: Omnia flumina intrant in mare, et mare non redundat; ad locum unde exeunt flumina revertuntur ut iterum fluant.

verses.text: All things are hard: man cannot explain them by word. The eye is not filled with seeing, neither is the ear filled with hearing.
verses.textLatin: Cunctæ res difficiles; non potest eas homo explicare sermone. Non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris auditu impletur.

verses.text: What is it that hath been? the same thing that shall be. What is it that hath been done? the same that shall be done.
verses.textLatin: Quid est quod fuit? Ipsum quod futurum est. Quid est quod factum est? Ipsum quod faciendum est.

verses.text: Nothing under the sun is new, neither is any man able to say: Behold this is new: for it hath already gone before in the ages that were before us.
verses.textLatin: Nihil sub sole novum, nec valet quisquam dicere: Ecce hoc recens est: jam enim præcessit in sæculis quæ fuerunt ante nos.

verses.text: There is no remembrance of former things: nor indeed of those things which hereafter are to come, shall there be any remembrance with them that shall be in the latter end.
verses.textLatin: Non est priorum memoria; sed nec eorum quidem quæ postea futura sunt erit recordatio apud eos qui futuri sunt in novissimo.

verses.text: I Ecclesiastes was king over Israel in Jerusalem,
verses.textLatin: Ego Ecclesiastes fui rex Israël in Jerusalem;

verses.text: And I proposed in my mind to seek and search out wisely concerning all things that are done under the sun. This painful occupation hath God given to the children of men, to be exercised therein.
verses.textLatin: et proposui in animo meo quærere et investigare sapienter de omnibus quæ fiunt sub sole. Hanc occupationem pessimam dedit Deus filiis hominum, ut occuparentur in ea.

verses.text: I have seen all things that are done under the sun, and behold all is vanity, and vexation of spirit.
verses.textLatin: Vidi cuncta quæ fiunt sub sole, et ecce universa vanitas et afflictio spiritus.

verses.text: The perverse are hard to be corrected, and the number of fools is infinite.
verses.textLatin: Perversi difficile corriguntur, et stultorum infinitus est numerus.

verses.text: I have spoken in my heart, saying: Behold I am become great, and have gone beyond all in wisdom, that were before me in Jerusalem: and my mind hath contemplated many things wisely, and I have learned.
verses.textLatin: Locutus sum in corde meo, dicens: Ecce magnus effectus sum, et præcessi omnes sapientia qui fuerunt ante me in Jerusalem; et mens mea contemplata est multa sapienter, et didici.

verses.text: And I have given my heart to know prudence, and learning, and errors, and folly: and I have perceived that in these also there was labour, and vexation of spirit,
verses.textLatin: Dedique cor meum ut scirem prudentiam atque doctrinam, erroresque et stultitiam; et agnovi quod in his quoque esset labor et afflictio spiritus:

verses.text: Because in much wisdom there is much indignation: and he that addeth knowledge, addeth also labour.
verses.textLatin: eo quod in multa sapientia multa sit indignatio; et qui addit scientiam, addit et laborem.

verses.text: I  SAID in my heart: I will go, and abound with delights, and enjoy good things. And I saw that this also was vanity.
verses.textLatin: Dixi ego in corde meo: Vadam, et affluam deliciis, et fruar bonis; et vidi quod hoc quoque esset vanitas.

verses.text: Laughter I counted error: and to mirth I said: Why art thou vainly deceived?
verses.textLatin: Risum reputavi errorem, et gaudio dixi: Quid frustra deciperis?

verses.text: I thought in my heart, to withdraw my flesh from wine, that I might turn my mind to wisdom, and might avoid folly, till I might see what was profitable for the children of men: and what they ought to do under the sun, all the days of their life.
verses.textLatin: Cogitavi in corde meo abstrahere a vino carnem meam, ut animam meam transferrem ad sapientiam, devitaremque stultitiam, donec viderem quid esset utile filiis hominum, quo facto opus est sub sole numero dierum vitæ suæ.

verses.text: I made me great works, I built me houses, and planted vineyards,
verses.textLatin: Magnificavi opera mea, ædificavi mihi domos, et plantavi vineas;

verses.text: I made gardens, and orchards, and set them with trees of all kinds,
verses.textLatin: feci hortos et pomaria, et consevi ea cuncti generis arboribus;

verses.text: And I made me ponds of water, to water therewith the wood of the young trees,
verses.textLatin: et exstruxi mihi piscinas aquarum, ut irrigarem silvam lignorum germinantium.

verses.text: I got me menservants, and maidservants, and had a great family: and herds of oxen, and great flocks of sheep, above all that were before me in Jerusalem:
verses.textLatin: Possedi servos et ancillas, multamque familiam habui: armenta quoque, et magnos ovium greges, ultra omnes qui fuerunt ante me in Jerusalem;

verses.text: I heaped together for myself silver and gold, and the wealth of kings, and provinces: I made me singing men, and singing women, and the delights of the sons of men, cups and vessels to serve to pour out wine:
verses.textLatin: coacervavi mihi argentum et aurum, et substantias regum ac provinciarum; feci mihi cantores et cantatrices, et delicias filiorum hominum, scyphos, et urceos in ministerio ad vina fundenda;

verses.text: And I surpassed in riches all that were before me in Jerusalem: my wisdom also remained with me.
verses.textLatin: et supergressus sum opibus omnes qui ante me fuerunt in Jerusalem: sapientia quoque perseveravit mecum.

verses.text: And whatsoever my eyes desired, I refused them not: and I withheld not my heart from enjoying every pleasure, and delighting itself in the things which I had prepared: and esteemed this my portion, to make use of my own labour.
verses.textLatin: Et omnia quæ desideraverunt oculi mei non negavi eis, nec prohibui cor meum quin omni voluptate frueretur, et oblectaret se in his quæ præparaveram; et hanc ratus sum partem meam si uterer labore meo.

verses.text: And when I turned myself to all the works which my hands had wrought, and to the labours wherein I had laboured in vain, I saw in all things vanity, and vexation of mind, and that nothing was lasting under the sun.
verses.textLatin: Cumque me convertissem ad universa opera quæ fecerant manus meæ, et ad labores in quibus frustra sudaveram, vidi in omnibus vanitatem et afflictionem animi, et nihil permanere sub sole.

verses.text: I passed further to behold wisdom, and errors and folly, (What is man, said I, that he can follow the King his maker?)
verses.textLatin: Transivi ad contemplandam sapientiam, erroresque, et stultitiam. (Quid est, inquam, homo, ut sequi possit regem, factorem suum?)

verses.text: And I saw that wisdom excelled folly, as much as light differeth from darkness.
verses.textLatin: Et vidi quod tantum præcederet sapientia stultitiam, quantum differt lux a tenebris.

verses.text: The eyes of a wise man are in his head: the fool walketh in darkness: and I learned that they were to die both alike.
verses.textLatin: Sapientis oculi in capite ejus; stultus in tenebris ambulat: et didici quod unus utriusque esset interitus.

verses.text: And I said in my heart: If the death of the fool and mine shall be one, what doth it avail me, that I have applied myself more to the study of wisdom? And speaking with my own mind, I perceived that this also was vanity.
verses.textLatin: Et dixi in corde meo: Si unus et stulti et meus occasus erit, quid mihi prodest quod majorem sapientiæ dedi operam? Locutusque cum mente mea, animadverti quod hoc quoque esset vanitas.

verses.text: For there shall be no remembrance of the wise no more than of the fool for ever, and the times to come shall cover all things together with oblivion: the learned dieth in like manner as the unlearned.
verses.textLatin: Non enim erit memoria sapientis similiter ut stulti in perpetuum, et futura tempora oblivione cuncta pariter operient: moritur doctus similiter ut indoctus.

verses.text: And therefore I was weary of my life, when I saw that all things under the sun are evil, and all vanity and vexation of spirit.
verses.textLatin: Et idcirco tæduit me vitæ meæ, videntem mala universa esse sub sole, et cuncta vanitatem et afflictionem spiritus.

verses.text: Again I hated all my application wherewith I had earnestly laboured under the sun, being like to have an heir after me,
verses.textLatin: Rursus detestatus sum omnem industriam meam, qua sub sole studiosissime laboravi, habiturus hæredem post me,

verses.text: Whom I know not whether he will be a wise man or a fool, and he shall have rule over all my labours with which I have laboured and been solicitous: and is there any thing so vain?
verses.textLatin: quem ignoro utrum sapiens an stultus futurus sit, et dominabitur in laboribus meis, quibus desudavi et sollicitus fui: et est quidquam tam vanum?

verses.text: Wherefore I left off and my heart renounced labouring any more under the sun.
verses.textLatin: Unde cessavi, renuntiavitque cor meum ultra laborare sub sole.

verses.text: For when a man laboureth in wisdom, and knowledge, and carefulness, he leaveth what he hath gotten to an idle man: so this also is vanity, and a great evil.
verses.textLatin: Nam cum alius laboret in sapientia, et doctrina, et sollicitudine, homini otioso quæsita dimittit; et hoc ergo vanitas et magnum malum.

verses.text: For what profit shall a man have of all his labour, and vexation of spirit, with which he hath been tormented under the sun?
verses.textLatin: Quid enim proderit homini de universo labore suo, et afflictione spiritus, qua sub sole cruciatus est?

verses.text: All his days are full of sorrows and miseries, even in the night he doth not rest in mind: and is not this vanity?
verses.textLatin: Cuncti dies ejus doloribus et ærumnis pleni sunt, nec per noctem mente requiescit. Et hoc nonne vanitas est?

verses.text: Is it not better to eat and drink, and to shew his soul good things of his labours? and this is from the hand of God.
verses.textLatin: Nonne melius est comedere et bibere, et ostendere animæ suæ bona de laboribus suis? et hoc de manu Dei est.

verses.text: Who shall so feast and abound with delights as I?
verses.textLatin: Quis ita devorabit et deliciis affluet ut ego?

verses.text: God hath given to a man that is good in his sight, wisdom, and knowledge, and joy: but to the sinner he hath given vexation, and superfluous care, to heap up and to gather together, and to give it to him that hath pleased God: but this also is vanity, and a fruitless solicitude of the mind.
verses.textLatin: Homini bono in conspectu suo dedit Deus sapientiam, et scientiam, et lætitiam; peccatori autem dedit afflictionem et curam superfluam, ut addat, et congreget, et tradat ei qui placuit Deo; sed et hoc vanitas est, et cassa sollicitudo mentis.

verses.text: All  things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven.
verses.textLatin: Omnia tempus habent, et suis spatiis transeunt universa sub cælo.

verses.text: A time to be born and a time to die. A time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted.
verses.textLatin: Tempus nascendi, et tempus moriendi; tempus plantandi, et tempus evellendi quod plantatum est.

verses.text: A time to kill, and a time to heal. A time to destroy, and a time to build.
verses.textLatin: Tempus occidendi, et tempus sanandi; tempus destruendi, et tempus ædificandi.

verses.text: A time to weep, and a time to laugh. A time to mourn, and a time to dance.
verses.textLatin: Tempus flendi, et tempus ridendi; tempus plangendi, et tempus saltandi.

verses.text: A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather. A time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces.
verses.textLatin: Tempus spargendi lapides, et tempus colligendi, tempus amplexandi, et tempus longe fieri ab amplexibus.

verses.text: A time to get, and a time to lose. A time to keep, and a time to cast away.
verses.textLatin: Tempus acquirendi, et tempus perdendi; tempus custodiendi, et tempus abjiciendi.

verses.text: A time to rend, and a time to sew. A time to keep silence, and a time to speak.
verses.textLatin: Tempus scindendi, et tempus consuendi; tempus tacendi, et tempus loquendi.

verses.text: A time of love, and a time of hatred. A time of war, and a time of peace.
verses.textLatin: Tempus dilectionis, et tempus odii; tempus belli, et tempus pacis.

verses.text: What hath man more of his labour?
verses.textLatin: Quid habet amplius homo de labore suo?

verses.text: I have seen the trouble, which God hath given the sons of men to be exercised in it.
verses.textLatin: Vidi afflictionem quam dedit Deus filiis hominum, ut distendantur in ea.

verses.text: He hath made all things good in their time, and hath delivered the world to their consideration, so that man cannot find out the work which God hath made from the beginning to the end.
verses.textLatin: Cuncta fecit bona in tempore suo, et mundum tradidit disputationi eorum, ut non inveniat homo opus quod operatus est Deus ab initio usque ad finem.

verses.text: And I have known that there was no better thing than to rejoice, and to do well in this life.
verses.textLatin: Et cognovi quod non esset melius nisi lætari, et facere bene in vita sua;

verses.text: For every man that eateth and drinketh, and seeth good of his labour, this is the gift of God.
verses.textLatin: omnis enim homo qui comedit et bibit, et videt bonum de labore suo, hoc donum Dei est.

verses.text: I have learned that all the works which God hath made, continue for ever: we cannot add any thing, nor take away from those things which God hath made that he may be feared.
verses.textLatin: Didici quod omnia opera quæ fecit Deus perseverent in perpetuum; non possumus eis quidquam addere, nec auferre, quæ fecit Deus ut timeatur.

verses.text: That which hath been made, the same continueth: the things that shall be, have already been: and God restoreth that which is past.
verses.textLatin: Quod factum est, ipsum permanet; quæ futura sunt jam fuerunt, et Deus instaurat quod abiit.

verses.text: I saw under the sun in the place of judgment wickedness, and in the place of justice iniquity.
verses.textLatin: Vidi sub sole in loco judicii impietatem, et in loco justitiæ iniquitatem:

verses.text: And I said in my heart: God shall judge both the just and the wicked, and then shall be the time of every thing.
verses.textLatin: et dixi in corde meo: Justum et impium judicabit Deus, et tempus omnis rei tunc erit.

verses.text: I said in my heart concerning the sons of men, that God would prove them, and shew them to be like beasts.
verses.textLatin: Dixi in corde meo de filiis hominum, ut probaret eos Deus, et ostenderet similes esse bestiis.

verses.text: Therefore the death of man, and of beasts is one, and the condition of them both is equal: as man dieth, so they also die: all things breathe alike, and man hath nothing more than beast: all things are subject to vanity.
verses.textLatin: Idcirco unus interitus est hominis et jumentorum, et æqua utriusque conditio. Sicut moritur homo, sic et illa moriuntur. Similiter spirant omnia, et nihil habet homo jumento amplius: cuncta subjacent vanitati,

verses.text: And all things go to one place: of earth they were made, and into earth they return together.
verses.textLatin: et omnia pergunt ad unum locum. De terra facta sunt, et in terram pariter revertuntur.

verses.text: Who knoweth if the spirit of the children of Adam ascend upward, and if the spirit of the beasts descend downward?
verses.textLatin: Quis novit si spiritus filiorum Adam ascendat sursum, et si spiritus jumentorum descendat deorsum?

verses.text: And I have found that nothing is better than for a man to rejoice in his work, and that this is his portion. For who shall bring him to know the things that shall be after him?
verses.textLatin: Et deprehendi nihil esse melius quam lætari hominem in opere suo, et hanc esse partem illius. Quis enim eum adducet ut post se futura cognoscat?

verses.text: I  TURNED myself to other things, and I saw the oppressions that are done under the sun, and the tears of the innocent, and they had no comforter; and they were not able to resist their violence, being destitute of help from any.
verses.textLatin: Verti me ad alia, et vidi calumnias quæ sub sole geruntur, et lacrimas innocentium, et neminem consolatorem, nec posse resistere eorum violentiæ, cunctorum auxilio destitutos,

verses.text: And I praised the dead rather than the living:
verses.textLatin: et laudavi magis mortuos quam viventes;

verses.text: And I judged him happier than them both, that is not yet born, nor hath seen the evils that are done under the sun.
verses.textLatin: et feliciorem utroque judicavi qui necdum natus est, nec vidit mala quæ sub sole fiunt.

verses.text: Again I considered all the labours of men, and I remarked that their industries are exposed to the envy of their neighbour: so in this also there is vanity, and fruitless care.
verses.textLatin: Rursum contemplatus sum omnes labores hominum, et industrias animadverti patere invidiæ proximi; et in hoc ergo vanitas et cura superflua est.

verses.text: The fool foldeth his hands together, and eateth his own flesh, saying:
verses.textLatin: Stultus complicat manus suas, et comedit carnes suas, dicens:

verses.text: Better is a handful with rest, than both hands full with labour, and vexation of mind.
verses.textLatin: Melior est pugillus cum requie, quam plena utraque manus cum labore et afflictione animi.

verses.text: Considering I found also another vanity under the sun:
verses.textLatin: Considerans, reperi et aliam vanitatem sub sole.

verses.text: There is but one, and he hath not a second, no child, no brother, and yet he ceaseth not to labour, neither are his eyes satisfied with riches, neither doth he reflect, saying: For whom do I labour, and defraud my soul of good things? in this also is vanity, and a grievous vexation.
verses.textLatin: Unus est, et secundum non habet, non filium, non fratrem, et tamen laborare non cessat, nec satiantur oculi ejus divitiis; nec recogitat, dicens: Cui laboro, et fraudo animam meam bonis? In hoc quoque vanitas est et afflictio pessima.

verses.text: It is better therefore that two should be together, than one: for they have the advantage of their society:
verses.textLatin: Melius est ergo duos esse simul quam unum; habent enim emolumentum societatis suæ.

verses.text: If one fall he shall be supported by the other: woe to him that is alone, for when he falleth, he hath none to lift him up.
verses.textLatin: Si unus ceciderit, ab altero fulcietur. Væ soli, quia cum ceciderit, non habet sublevantem se.

verses.text: And if two lie together, they shall warm one another: how shall one alone be warmed?
verses.textLatin: Et si dormierint duo, fovebuntur mutuo; unus quomodo calefiet?

verses.text: And if a man prevail against one, two shall withstand him: a threefold cord is not easily broken.
verses.textLatin: Et si quispiam prævaluerit contra unum, duo resistunt ei; funiculus triplex difficile rumpitur.

verses.text: Better is a child that is poor and wise, than a king that is old and foolish, who knoweth not to foresee for hereafter.
verses.textLatin: Melior est puer pauper et sapiens, rege sene et stulto, qui nescit prævidere in posterum.

verses.text: Because out of prison and chains sometimes a man cometh forth to a kingdom: and another born king is consumed with poverty.
verses.textLatin: Quod de carcere catenisque interdum quis egrediatur ad regnum; et alius, natus in regno, inopia consumatur.

verses.text: I saw all men living, that walk under the sun with the second young man, who shall rise up in his place.
verses.textLatin: Vidi cunctos viventes qui ambulant sub sole cum adolescente secundo, qui consurget pro eo.

verses.text: The number of the people, of all that were before him is infinite: and they that shall come afterwards, shall not rejoice in him: but this also is vanity, and vexation of spirit.
verses.textLatin: Infinitus numerus est populi omnium qui fuerunt ante eum, et qui postea futuri sunt non lætabuntur in eo; sed et hoc vanitas et afflictio spiritus.

verses.text: Keep thy foot, when thou goest into the house of God, and draw nigh to hear. For much better is obedience, than the victims of fools, who know not what evil they do.
verses.textLatin: Custodi pedem tuum ingrediens domum Dei, et appropinqua ut audias. Multo enim melior est obedientia quam stultorum victimæ, qui nesciunt quid faciunt mali.

verses.text: Speak  not any thing rashly, and let not thy heart be hasty to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few.
verses.textLatin: Ne temere quid loquaris, neque cor tuum sit velox ad proferendum sermonem coram Deo. Deus enim in cælo, et tu super terram; idcirco sint pauci sermones tui.

verses.text: Dreams follow many cares: and in many words shall be found folly.
verses.textLatin: Multas curas sequuntur somnia, et in multis sermonibus invenietur stultitia.

verses.text: If thou hast vowed any thing to God, defer not to pay it: for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeaseth him: but whatsoever thou hast vowed, pay it.
verses.textLatin: Si quid vovisti Deo, ne moreris reddere: displicet enim ei infidelis et stulta promissio, sed quodcumque voveris redde:

verses.text: And it is much better not to vow, than after a vow not to perform the things promised.
verses.textLatin: multoque melius est non vovere, quam post votum promissa non reddere.

verses.text: Give not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin: and say not before the angel: There is no providence: lest God be angry at thy words, and destroy all the works of thy hands.
verses.textLatin: Ne dederis os tuum ut peccare facias carnem tuam, neque dicas coram angelo: Non est providentia: ne forte iratus Deus contra sermones tuos dissipet cuncta opera manuum tuarum.

verses.text: Where there are many dreams, there are many vanities, and words without number: but do thou fear God.
verses.textLatin: Ubi multa sunt somnia, plurimæ sunt vanitates, et sermones innumeri; tu vero Deum time.

verses.text: If thou shalt see the oppressions of the poor, and violent judgments, and justice perverted in the province, wonder not at this matter: for he that is high hath another higher, and there are others still higher than these:
verses.textLatin: Si videris calumnias egenorum, et violenta judicia, et subverti justitiam in provincia, non mireris super hoc negotio: quia excelso excelsior est alius, et super hos quoque eminentiores sunt alii;

verses.text: Moreover there is the king that reigneth over all the land subject to him.
verses.textLatin: et insuper universæ terræ rex imperat servienti.

verses.text: A covetous man shall not be satisfied with money: and he that loveth riches shall reap no fruit from them: so this also is vanity.
verses.textLatin: Avarus non implebitur pecunia, et qui amat divitias fructum non capiet ex eis; et hoc ergo vanitas.

verses.text: Where there are great riches, there are also many to eat them. And what doth it profit the owner, but that he seeth the riches with his eyes?
verses.textLatin: Ubi multæ sunt opes, multi et qui comedunt eas. Et quid prodest possessori, nisi quod cernit divitias oculis suis?

verses.text: Sleep is sweet to a labouring man, whether he eat little or much: but the fulness of the rich will not suffer him to sleep.
verses.textLatin: Dulcis est somnus operanti, sive parum sive multum comedat; saturitas autem divitis non sinit eum dormire.

verses.text: There is also another grievous evil, which I have seen under the sun: riches kept to the hurt of the owner.
verses.textLatin: Est et alia infirmitas pessima quam vidi sub sole: divitiæ conservatæ in malum domini sui.

verses.text: For they are lost with very great affliction: he hath begotten a son, who shall be in extremity of want.
verses.textLatin: Pereunt enim in afflictione pessima: generavit filium qui in summa egestate erit.

verses.text: As he came forth naked from his mother’s womb, so shall he return, and shall take nothing away with him of his labour.
verses.textLatin: Sicut egressus est nudus de utero matris suæ, sic revertetur, et nihil auferet secum de labore suo.

verses.text: A most deplorable evil: as he came, so shall he return. What then doth it profit him that he hath laboured for the wind?
verses.textLatin: Miserabilis prorsus infirmitas: quomodo venit, sic revertetur. Quid ergo prodest ei quod laboravit in ventum?

verses.text: All the days of his life he eateth in darkness, and in many cares, and in misery, and sorrow.
verses.textLatin: cunctis diebus vitæ suæ comedit in tenebris, et in curis multis, et in ærumna atque tristitia.

verses.text: This therefore hath seemed good to me, that a man should eat and drink, and enjoy the fruit of his labour, wherewith he hath laboured under the sun, all the days of his life, which God hath given him: and this is his portion.
verses.textLatin: Hoc itaque visum est mihi bonum, ut comedat quis et bibat, et fruatur lætitia ex labore suo quo laboravit ipse sub sole, numero dierum vitæ suæ quos dedit ei Deus; et hæc est pars illius.

verses.text: And every man to whom God hath given riches, and substance, and hath given him power to eat thereof, and to enjoy his portion, and to rejoice of his labour: this is the gift of God.
verses.textLatin: Et omni homini cui dedit Deus divitias atque substantiam, potestatemque ei tribuit ut comedat ex eis, et fruatur parte sua, et lætetur de labore suo: hoc est donum Dei.

verses.text: For he shall not much remember the days of his life, because God entertaineth his heart with delight.
verses.textLatin: Non enim satis recordabitur dierum vitæ suæ, eo quod Deus occupet deliciis cor ejus.

verses.text: There  is also another evil, which I have seen under the sun, and that frequent among men:
verses.textLatin: Est et aliud malum quod vidi sub sole, et quidem frequens apud homines:

verses.text: A man to whom God hath given riches, and substance, and honour, and his soul wanteth nothing of all that he desireth: yet God doth not give him power to eat thereof, but a stranger shall eat it up. This is vanity and a great misery.
verses.textLatin: vir cui dedit Deus divitias, et substantiam, et honorem, et nihil deest animæ suæ ex omnibus quæ desiderat; nec tribuit ei potestatem Deus ut comedat ex eo, sed homo extraneus vorabit illud: hoc vanitas et miseria magna est.

verses.text: If a man beget a hundred children, and live many years, and attain to a great age, and his soul make no use of the goods of his substance, and he be without burial: of this man I pronounce, that the untimely born is better than he.
verses.textLatin: Si genuerit quispiam centum liberos, et vixerit multos annos, et plures dies ætatis habuerit, et anima illius non utatur bonis substantiæ suæ, sepulturaque careat: de hoc ergo pronuntio quod melior illo sit abortivus.

verses.text: For he came in vain, and goeth to darkness, and his name shall be wholly forgotten.
verses.textLatin: Frustra enim venit, et pergit ad tenebras, et oblivione delebitur nomen ejus.

verses.text: He hath not seen the sun, nor known the distance of good and evil:
verses.textLatin: Non vidit solem, neque cognovit distantiam boni et mali.

verses.text: Although he lived two thousand years, and hath not enjoyed good things: do not all make haste to one place?
verses.textLatin: Etiam si duobus millibus annis vixerit, et non fuerit perfruitus bonis, nonne ad unum locum properant omnia?

verses.text: All the labour of man is for his mouth, but his soul shall not be filled.
verses.textLatin: Omnis labor hominis in ore ejus; sed anima ejus non implebitur.

verses.text: What hath the wise man more than the fool? and what the poor man, but to go thither, where there is life?
verses.textLatin: Quid habet amplius sapiens a stulto? et quid pauper, nisi ut pergat illuc ubi est vita?

verses.text: Better it is to see what thou mayst desire, than to desire that which thou canst not know. But this also is vanity, and presumption of spirit.
verses.textLatin: Melius est videre quod cupias, quam desiderare quod nescias. Sed et hoc vanitas est, et præsumptio spiritus.

verses.text: He that shall be, his name is already called: and it is known, that he is man, and cannot contend in judgment with him that is stronger than himself.
verses.textLatin: Qui futurus est, jam vocatum est nomen ejus; et scitur quod homo sit, et non possit contra fortiorem se in judicio contendere.

verses.text: There are many words that have much vanity in disputing.
verses.textLatin: Verba sunt plurima, multamque in disputando habentia vanitatem.

verses.text: What  needeth a man to seek things that are above him, whereas he knoweth not what is profitable for him in his life, in all the days of his pilgrimage, and the time that passeth like a shadow? Or who can tell him what shall be after him under the sun?
verses.textLatin: Quid necesse est homini majora se quærere, cum ignoret quid conducat sibi in vita sua, numero dierum peregrinationis suæ, et tempore quod velut umbra præterit? aut quis ei poterit indicare quod post eum futurum sub sole sit?

verses.text: A good name is better than precious ointments: and the day of death than the day of one’s birth.
verses.textLatin: Melius est nomen bonum quam unguenta pretiosa, et dies mortis die nativitatis.

verses.text: It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to the house of feasting: for in that we are put in mind of the end of all, and the living thinketh what is to come.
verses.textLatin: Melius est ire ad domum luctus quam ad domum convivii; in illa enim finis cunctorum admonetur hominum, et vivens cogitat quid futurum sit.

verses.text: Anger is better than laughter: because by the sadness of the countenance the mind of the offender is corrected.
verses.textLatin: Melior est ira risu, quia per tristitiam vultus corrigitur animus delinquentis.

verses.text: The heart of the wise is where there is mourning, and the heart of fools where there is mirth.
verses.textLatin: Cor sapientium ubi tristitia est, et cor stultorum ubi lætitia.

verses.text: It is better to be rebuked by a wise man, than to be deceived by the flattery of fools.
verses.textLatin: Melius est a sapiente corripi, quam stultorum adulatione decipi;

verses.text: For as the crackling of thorns burning under a pot, so is the laughter of a fool: now this also is vanity.
verses.textLatin: quia sicut sonitus spinarum ardentium sub olla, sic risus stulti. Sed et hoc vanitas.

verses.text: Oppression troubleth the wise, and shall destroy the strength of his heart.
verses.textLatin: Calumnia conturbat sapientem, et perdet robur cordis illius.

verses.text: Better is the end of a speech than the beginning. Better is the patient man than the presumptuous.
verses.textLatin: Melior est finis orationis quam principium. Melior est patiens arrogante.

verses.text: Be not quickly angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of a fool.
verses.textLatin: Ne sis velox ad irascendum, quia ira in sinu stulti requiescit.

verses.text: Say not: What thinkest thou is the cause that former times were better than they are now? for this manner of question is foolish.
verses.textLatin: Ne dicas: Quid putas causæ est quod priora tempora meliora fuere quam nunc sunt? stulta enim est hujuscemodi interrogatio.

verses.text: Wisdom with riches is more profitable, and bringeth more advantage to them that see the sun.
verses.textLatin: Utilior est sapientia cum divitiis, et magis prodest videntibus solem.

verses.text: For as wisdom is a defence, so money is a defence: but learning and wisdom excel in this, that they give life to him that possesseth them.
verses.textLatin: Sicut enim protegit sapientia, sic protegit pecunia; hoc autem plus habet eruditio et sapientia, quod vitam tribuunt possessori suo.

verses.text: Consider the works of God, that no man can correct whom he hath despised.
verses.textLatin: Considera opera Dei, quod nemo possit corrigere quem ille despexerit.

verses.text: In the good day enjoy good things, and beware beforehand of the evil day: for God hath made both the one and the other, that man may not find against him any just complaint.
verses.textLatin: In die bona fruere bonis, et malam diem præcave; sicut enim hanc, sic et illam fecit Deus, ut non inveniat homo contra eum justas querimonias.

verses.text: These things also I saw in the days of my vanity: A just man perisheth in his justice, and a wicked man liveth a long time in his wickedness.
verses.textLatin: Hæc quoque vidi in diebus vanitatis meæ: justus perit in justitia sua, et impius multo vivit tempore in malitia sua.

verses.text: Be not over just: and be not more wise than is necessary, lest thou become stupid.
verses.textLatin: Noli esse justus multum, neque plus sapias quam necesse est, ne obstupescas.

verses.text: Be not overmuch wicked: and be not foolish, lest thou die before thy time.
verses.textLatin: Ne impie agas multum, et noli esse stultus, ne moriaris in tempore non tuo.

verses.text: It is good that thou shouldst hold up the just, yea and from him withdraw not thy hand: for he that feareth God, neglecteth nothing.
verses.textLatin: Bonum est te sustentare justum: sed et ab illo ne subtrahas manum tuam; quia qui timet Deum nihil negligit.

verses.text: Wisdom hath strengthened the wise more than ten princes of the city.
verses.textLatin: Sapientia confortavit sapientem super decem principes civitatis;

verses.text: For there is no just man upon earth, that doth good, and sinneth not.
verses.textLatin: non est enim homo justus in terra qui faciat bonum et non peccet.

verses.text: But do not apply thy heart to all words that are spoken: lest perhaps thou hear thy servant reviling thee.
verses.textLatin: Sed et cunctis sermonibus qui dicuntur ne accomodes cor tuum, ne forte audias servum tuum maledicentem tibi;

verses.text: For thy conscience knoweth that thou also hast often spoken evil of others.
verses.textLatin: scit enim conscientia tua quia et tu crebro maledixisti aliis.

verses.text: I have tried all things in wisdom. I have said: I will be wise: and it departed farther from me,
verses.textLatin: Cuncta tentavi in sapientia. Dixi: Sapiens efficiar: et ipsa longius recessit a me,

verses.text: Much more than it was: it is a great depth, who shall find it out?
verses.textLatin: multo magis quam erat. Et alta profunditas, quis inveniet eam?

verses.text: I have surveyed all things with my mind, to know, and consider, and seek out wisdom and reason: and to know the wickedness of the fool, and the error of the imprudent:
verses.textLatin: Lustravi universa animo meo, ut scirem et considerarem, et quærerem sapientiam, et rationem, et ut cognoscerem impietatem stulti, et errorem imprudentium:

verses.text: And I have found a woman more bitter than death, who is the hunter’s snare, and her heart is a net, and her hands are bands. He that pleaseth God shall escape from her: but he that is a sinner, shall be caught by her.
verses.textLatin: et inveni amariorem morte mulierem, quæ laqueus venatorum est, et sagena cor ejus; vincula sunt manus illius. Qui placet Deo effugiet illam; qui autem peccator est capietur ab illa.

verses.text: Lo this have I found, said Ecclesiastes, weighing one thing after another, that I might find out the account,
verses.textLatin: Ecce hoc inveni, dixit Ecclesiastes, unum et alterum ut invenirem rationem,

verses.text: Which yet my soul seeketh, and I have not found it. One man among a thousand I have found, a woman among them all I have not found.
verses.textLatin: quam adhuc quærit anima mea, et non inveni. Virum de mille unum reperi; mulierem ex omnibus non inveni.

verses.text: Only this I have found, that God made man right, and he hath entangled himself with an infinity of questions. Who is as the wise man? and who hath known the resolution of the word?
verses.textLatin: Solummodo hoc inveni, quod fecerit Deus hominem rectum, et ipse se infinitis miscuerit quæstionibus. Quis talis ut sapiens est? et quis cognovit solutionem verbi?

verses.text: The  wisdom of a man shineth in his countenance, and the most mighty will change his face.
verses.textLatin: Sapientia hominis lucet in vultu ejus, et potentissimus faciem illius commutabit.

verses.text: I observe the mouth of the king, and the commandments of the oath of God.
verses.textLatin: Ego os regis observo, et præcepta juramenti Dei.

verses.text: Be not hasty to depart from his face, and do not continue in an evil work: for he will do all that pleaseth him:
verses.textLatin: Ne festines recedere a facie ejus, neque permaneas in opere malo: quia omne quod voluerit faciet.

verses.text: And his word is full of power: neither can any man say to him: Why dost thou so?
verses.textLatin: Et sermo illius potestate plenus est, nec dicere ei quisquam potest: Quare ita facis?

verses.text: He that keepeth the commandment, shall find no evil. The heart of a wise man understandeth time and answer.
verses.textLatin: Qui custodit præceptum non experietur quidquam mali. Tempus et responsionem cor sapientis intelligit.

verses.text: There is a time and opportunity for every business, and great affliction for man:
verses.textLatin: Omni negotio tempus est, et opportunitas: et multa hominis afflictio,

verses.text: Because he is ignorant of things past, and things to come he cannot know by any messenger.
verses.textLatin: quia ignorat præterita, et futura nullo scire potest nuntio.

verses.text: It is not in man’s power to stop the spirit, neither hath he power in the day of death, neither is he suffered to rest when war is at hand, neither shall wickedness save the wicked.
verses.textLatin: Non est in hominis potestate prohibere spiritum, nec habet potestatem in die mortis: nec sinitur quiescere ingruente bello, neque salvabit impietas impium.

verses.text: All these things I have considered, and applied my heart to all the works that are done under the sun. Sometimes one man ruleth over another to his own hurt.
